tier_rationale: The Impact Sport R-01526 is an analog electronic earmuff: built-in directional microphones amplify ambient sound up to 4x and compress it back down once it hits 82dB, entirely as a local audio circuit with no data radio of any kind. Honeywell's own grantee (2AJKI) files FCC intentional-radiator grants for its Bluetooth-equipped hearing protection -- 'Impact Sport Bluetooth' (2AJKI-ISEMBT) and two in-ear Bluetooth models (2AJKI-ISINBT, 2AJKI-ISINHTBT) -- but the plain, non-Bluetooth Impact Sport R-01526 has no FCC filing under that grantee at all. That is the sibling-control pattern: this vendor demonstrably files when a model has a radio, and the absence for this model is meaningful rather than a search miss.
the_unplug_test: Nothing changes, because nothing was ever connected. The earmuffs run on two AAA batteries and use a local amplify-and-compress circuit to let range commands and conversation through while clamping down hard, sudden noise -- the same behavior on day one and after ten years, with or without a phone, an app, or an internet connection anywhere nearby. There is no pairing, no account, and no firmware to update.

repairability.notes: User-replaceable 2x AAA batteries behind a snap-on compartment lid, per the manufacturer's own product description.

sources.supports: Full grant list for grantee Honeywell Safety Products USA, Inc. (2AJKI): five grants total, all for named Bluetooth or telemetry products (Impact Sport Bluetooth, two in-ear Bluetooth hearing-protection models, a firefighter telemetry system, and 'Sync Wireless'). No grant exists for a plain/non-Bluetooth Impact Sport model -- the sibling control establishing that the vendor files when a model has a radio, making the absence for R-01526 meaningful.

Confirms FCC ID 2AJKI-ISEMBT, 'Impact Sport Bluetooth', 2402-2480 MHz, filed by Honeywell Safety Products USA in 2021 -- the Bluetooth sibling model whose existence makes the plain model's lack of a grant meaningful rather than a search gap.

Manufacturer-affiliated retail listing for the plain (non-Bluetooth) Impact Sport Electronic Earmuffs: describes built-in directional microphones amplifying ambient sound to a safe 82dB, amplification up to 4x, automatic compression above 82dB, 22dB passive NRR, 4-hour auto shut-off, and no mention of Bluetooth or wireless features anywhere in the product description -- distinct listing from the separately-sold 'Bluetooth Impact Sport' model.

open_questions: Exact current US retail price per single unit (as opposed to the 5-pack case price seen) was not independently confirmed within budget; price_band is estimated from typical single-unit listings seen across retailers, not a single authoritative figure.

Model number, NRR rating and battery type were originally corroborated from an aggregated search page, which has been removed as not being a source. These details are not load-bearing for the D0 — that rests on the FCC sibling-control absence — but they are now carried by the Honeywell store listing alone and would benefit from the printed manual.
notes: Chosen deliberately as the receiver-and-amplifier-only case, parallel to the Casio Wave Ceptor records already in the catalog: 'electronic hearing protection' sounds high-tech but the amplification is a local analog audio circuit, not a radio, and this exact product line demonstrates the point by selling a nearly identical Bluetooth sibling under a clearly different model name. First record in the empty 'hearing protection' subcategory.
